Pseudo-spectral vs. Finite-Difference Solvers

Relative accuracy of numerical schemes for long-time turbulence simulation.

Pseudo-spectral methods are the standard for simulating turbulence in periodic domains. Their derivatives are exact for resolved fields, and a finite-difference (FD) scheme needs roughly six times more grid points per direction to match their accuracy. But spectral codes scale poorly: every 3-D FFT needs all-to-all communication between processors, and walls and complex geometries are hard to handle. FD codes need only nearest-neighbour communication and handle walls naturally.

So does the extra accuracy of a single spectral time step actually show up over a long turbulence simulation? This work, done at IIT Kanpur with Prof. Mahendra K. Verma and Dr. Shashwat Bhattacharya, says largely no.

Setup

  • Flow: forced homogeneous turbulence in a \((2\pi)^3\) periodic box on a \(256^3\) grid, driven by Taylor–Green forcing at Reynolds numbers 965, 1231, 1515 and 1994.
  • Solvers: Py-Tarang (pseudo-spectral) and Py-Saras (second-order central FD on a staggered grid, with a geometric-multigrid pressure Poisson solver). Both are Python codes accelerated on GPUs with CuPy.
  • Fair comparison: both solvers start from the same fully developed turbulent field and use the same RK3 time stepping (\(\Delta t = 0.001\)) for 100 time units.
  • Cost: about 0.8 s per step for the spectral code and 1.5 s for the FD code on one NVIDIA RTX 3090. The multigrid pressure solve makes FD slower on a single GPU, but on many GPUs the FFT’s all-to-all communication is expected to reverse that.

Findings

Same energy, same statistics. The time-averaged kinetic energies from the two solvers agree to within about 4% at every Reynolds number. The flow structures are not identical, because the solutions diverge as numerical errors grow, but they are statistically the same: similar vortex sizes and densities, and nearly identical PDFs of velocity and velocity gradients.

Vertical vorticity with horizontal velocity vectors on the midplane at \(t = 60\) for the four Reynolds numbers: (a) pseudo-spectral and (b) finite-difference solver.

Same spectra and fluxes. Energy spectra and energy fluxes from the two codes lie on top of each other across the energy-containing and inertial ranges. The only difference is a small kink near \(k \approx 100\) in the FD spectra, where energy piles up at the smallest resolved scales.

Energy spectra \(E(k)\) (pseudo-spectral: solid blue; finite difference: dashed red) for the four Reynolds numbers, with the energy flux \(\Pi(k)\) in the insets.

Why it works

A statistically steady turbulent flow lives on an attractor in phase space. Both solvers produce trajectories confined to that attractor. Instead of piling up, the per-step numerical errors largely cancel, so both codes sample the same statistics even though their trajectories differ. This is similar to the shadowing lemma for chaotic systems.

The practical point is that FD solvers are a credible, more scalable alternative for very large turbulence simulations, where FFT communication dominates the cost. I see this directly in my multi-GPU spectral code, where data transposes take about a third of each time step (more on my SC’26 page).

Publication

  • A. Rodhiya, S. Bhattacharya and M. K. Verma, “Relative accuracy of turbulence simulations using pseudo-spectral and finite difference solvers,” Sādhanā 51, 38 (2026). doi:10.1007/s12046-025-03035-y
